methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective cohort study (N=12,096 women; complete data N=7,191) using hospital cancer registry linked to state mortality system (2000-2016, follow-up through 2021). Appropriate statistical methods: Kaplan-Meier survival, cause-specific Cox proportional hazards with complete-case analysis (40.5% missing multivariable data). No randomization, no blinding. Confounding adjustment attempted via multivariable model. However, missing data handling not discussed; selection bias inherent in healthcare system segmentation (public vs. private pathways).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Retrospective cohort (LoE 2b) of breast cancer patients from statewide oncology network. Direct clinical relevance: 5-year survival 97% (stage I) to 32% (stage IV); identifies healthcare access disparities (private system HR 0.83 vs. public, P=0.001). Highlights need for early detection strategies. Limited by lack of intervention, no mechanistic insights.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE adherence reasonable: describes setting (Oncology Care Network of Espírito Santo), inclusion/exclusion criteria, variables clearly defined, outcomes specified, statistical methods described. However, flow diagram absent, missing data mechanisms not explained (40.5% excluded from multivariable), no statement on data availability. Multi-site study with standardized registry likely enables reproducibility but no explicit data sharing statement.

novelty_literature.justification: Breast cancer survival strongly determined by stage well-established. Present study documents stage-dependent survival in Brazilian statewide cohort—incremental confirmation in new population. Healthcare access/referral pathway effect (public vs. private) clinically relevant but not novel mechanistically. No new biomarkers, pathways, or treatment strategies identified.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized: Introduction contextualizes Brazilian health disparities, Methods detail registry linkage methodology, Results present stage-stratified survival curves with Kaplan-Meier estimates, Discussion addresses structural healthcare factors. Clearly written; Table/Figure references support main text. Minor issue: extensive missing data (40.5%) acknowledged as limitation but impact on inference not fully discussed.

key_strengths: Large statewide cohort (N=12,096) spanning all oncology centers, capturing real-world healthcare segmentation (public vs. private systems) in middle-income setting
Linked registry-mortality data enables accurate cancer-specific survival estimation; comprehensive follow-up through 2021 (up to 21 years)
Clear stage-dependent survival gradient: Stage I 97% vs. Stage IV 32% (5-year), clinically meaningful
Identifies actionable healthcare disparity: Private system referral associated with lower mortality (HR 0.83, P=0.001), highlighting access inequity
key_concerns: 40.5% data loss in multivariable analysis (7,191/12,096) due to missing key variables (TNM, disease status, treatment rationale); complete-case analysis may introduce bias
No mechanistic insights or novel findings—stage-dependent survival already well-established
Healthcare access differences confounded by unmeasured factors (socioeconomic status, timeliness of referral, treatment intensity); study design cannot disentangle causation from selection
No data availability statement; reproducibility of linkage procedures unclear
chief_reviewer.rationale: Solid epidemiologic surveillance study documenting breast cancer outcomes in Brazilian state-level network with emphasis on healthcare access disparities. Appropriate for public health/oncology journals with minor revisions addressing missing data mechanisms and health equity implications.
